title: Equity reads adversaries where they speak calmly, and softens harsh dispute-talk from better places
source_text: VIII. Porro licet ista sic temere effutita, odioque et caeco affectu, potius quam certa animi sententia prolata, justissime a nostris notentur et exagitentur: in constituendo tamen controversiae alicujus statu, respiciendum potius arbitramur ad ea loca ubi sedato animo loquuntur, et rem illam, de qua agitur, ex professo tractant, mentemque suae Ecclesiae clare et distincte explicant. Etenim, non tantum istiusmodi viris, qui malam causam agunt, sed viris quoque bonis, quibus propositum est veritatem tueri, non raro contingit ut, inter disputandum, ab adversa sententia plus nimio recedant, et deferantur in contrarias oras; eaque imprudenter proferant in adversarium, quae ipsis quoque nocent, neque cum veritate, et propriis ipsorum placitis usquequaque congruunt. Quod tam nostri quam Pontificii saepe in priscis Ecclesiae Patribus animadvertunt, dum schismaticos et haereticos confutant et in haereses invehuntur. Sed aequitas et candor exigit, ut quae ita duriter et incommode dicta sunt, explicentur ex aliis locis, ubi autores illi commodius loquuntur, et veritati magis consentanee. Neque diffitemur nostros quoque Doctores aliquando hac venia et indulgentia egere. Ideoque, ut benigne et candide agamus cum adversariis nostris, existimamus etiam hoc ipsis debere concedi, ut sicubi quaedam male et falso prolocuti sint, alibi vero bene et veritati congruenter, priora illa ex posterioribus emolliantur et intelligantur.
pass_a_gloss: Furthermore, although those things thus rashly blurted out, and brought forth by hatred and blind passion rather than by a settled judgment of the mind, may most justly be noted and agitated by our people: yet in establishing the state of any controversy, we think we should rather look to those places where they speak with a calm mind, and treat the matter in question from profession, and clearly and distinctly explain the mind of their Church. For it happens not rarely not only to men of that sort who plead a bad cause, but also to good men whose purpose is to defend the truth, that in disputing they withdraw too far from the adverse opinion and are carried into opposite regions; and imprudently bring forward against an adversary things that also harm themselves, and do not altogether agree with the truth and with their own opinions. Which both our people and the Pontificii often observe in the ancient Fathers of the Church, while they refute schismatics and heretics and inveigh against heresies. But equity and candor require that things said thus harshly and awkwardly be explained from other places where those authors speak more conveniently and more in agreement with the truth. Nor do we deny that our Doctors too sometimes need this pardon and indulgence. And therefore, that we may deal kindly and candidly with our adversaries, we judge that this also ought to be granted to them: that if anywhere they have spoken certain things badly and falsely, but elsewhere well and in agreement with the truth, the former may be softened and understood from the latter.
pass_b_english: Those rash blurted words, born of hatred and blind passion rather than a settled judgment, our people may most justly note and press. Yet when we fix the state of any controversy, we think we should look rather to the places where they speak with a calm mind, treat the matter on purpose, and explain their Church's mind clearly and distinctly.

Not only men who plead a bad cause, but also good men set on defending the truth, often pull too far from the opposing view in the heat of dispute and are carried to the opposite shore. They imprudently urge against an adversary things that also hurt themselves, and that do not sit fully with the truth or with their own settled opinions. Our people and the Pontificii alike often notice this in the ancient Fathers of the Church, when those Fathers refute schismatics and heretics and inveigh against heresies.

Equity and candor require that words spoken so harshly and awkwardly be explained from other places where those authors speak more fitly and more in step with the truth. We do not deny that our own doctors sometimes need the same pardon and indulgence. So if we are to deal kindly and candidly with our adversaries, we judge that the same should be granted them: where they have spoken badly and falsely in one place, but well and truly in another, the earlier words should be softened and read from the later.

choices.why: They treat the question deliberately in calm loci, not only in polemic asides.
Earlier harsh talk is tempered by later clearer teaching.
